sections.h: Book 3: Antonius invades Italy, Vitellius falls
sections.b: Book 3 of the Histories is the Flavianist conquest of Italy. Primus Antonius leads the Danube legions across the Alps (3:1-3:8); Caecina's Vitellianist army breaks up in treason (3:12-3:14); the second battle at Bedriacum is won at night near Cremona, which is then stormed and sacked (3:15-3:34). Wikipedia dates the battle to 24 October 69. Vitellius gives up the throne on 18 December (3:67), the Capitol burns (3:71), and he is killed two days later (Wikipedia gives 20 December). Domitian is hailed as Caesar in the last line (3:86).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:1-3:86

common: The Flavianist side won because the Danube legions struck before the East could join them.
uncommon: Wikipedia's article on the year says some scholars argue that the new regime distorted the events, especially through the writings of the historian Tacitus.

sections.b: Marcus Antonius Primus is the main figure of Book 3. A man from Tolosa in Gaul (Suetonius, Vitellius 18), convicted of forgery under Nero and put over the 7th legion by Galba (Tacitus 2:86), he speaks for striking at once (3:2), wins the soldiers (3:3), calms two mutinies (3:10-3:11), wins at Cremona (3:15-3:29) and holds the army back from a night attack (3:20). Tacitus also blames him for the sack of Cremona, for building himself a road to power after it (3:49), and for his quarrel with Mucianus (3:52-3:53). The Senate gave him consular rank; he left Rome when Mucianus arrived (Wikipedia). Josephus names him with Mucianus as a destroyer of Vitellius's army (War 4.495) and has him allow his soldiers to plunder Cremona (War 4.11.3).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:2-3:3; Histories of Tacitus 3:20; Histories of Tacitus 3:49; Histories of Tacitus 3:53

sections.b: Tacitus calls Flavius Sabinus the prefect of the city and Vespasian's elder brother. He is urged to act (3:64), meets Vitellius in the temple of Apollo (3:65), takes the Capitol after Vitellius's abdication (3:69), and is taken and killed after the fire (3:73-3:74). Tacitus sums up his life: 35 years of service, 7 as governor of Moesia and 12 as prefect of the city, with one fault, that he talked too much (3:75). Josephus agrees that he seized the Capitol by night (War 4.645).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:64-3:65; Histories of Tacitus 3:69; Histories of Tacitus 3:73-3:75

sections.b: The Capitol was the hill of Rome's chief temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest, with Juno and Minerva beside him (Wikipedia). In December 69 Flavius Sabinus held the citadel against the Vitellianist soldiers, who set the gates alight and fought up the hill; the temple burned. Tacitus says it was doubtful which side started the fire. Josephus and Dio put it on Vitellius's soldiers, Suetonius on Vitellius himself, and Plutarch names no cause. Tacitus lists the temple's earlier history in 3:72 and calls its loss the saddest and most shameful thing to happen to the republic since the city was founded.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:69-3:72; Histories of Tacitus 3:74

sections.b: Vespasian began the rebuilding and the temple was dedicated in AD 75. A fire in AD 80 destroyed it, and Domitian's temple was finished in AD 82 (Wikipedia).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:72

claude.title: A pair of fires
claude.body: Claude's own theory, set out in full on the chapter page for Book 3. In short: the Capitol burned in December 69 and the Jerusalem temple burned the next year, but the two fires belonged to opposite sides of the civil war, Vitellius's German soldiers and Titus's eastern army. Tacitus records another ancient reading of the Capitol fire, the Gauls' and Druids' belief that it was a sign of heaven's anger (4:54).
claude.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:71-3:72; Histories of Tacitus 4:54; Mark 13:2; Luke 21:6

sections.b: Cremona was a Roman colony on the Padus, founded, Tacitus says, in the consulship of Tiberius Sempronius and Publius Cornelius, 286 years before AD 69 (3:34). The second battle of Bedriacum ended with the storming of the Vitellianist camp beside its walls (3:26-3:29) and the town's surrender (3:30-3:31). The soldiers then sacked the city for four days, and only the temple of Mefitis outside the walls stood (3:33). Antonius afterward forbade keeping Cremonans as captives; the town was rebuilt and Vespasian encouraged it (3:34).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:26-3:34

sections.b: Tacitus shows Vitellius idle in his gardens (3:36), hiding the news of Cremona (3:54), leaving Rome for Mevania and drifting back (3:55-3:56), giving up the throne in the Forum on 18 December (3:67-3:68), and driven back by the crowd to the Palace (3:68). He was found hiding, led through the city and killed at the Gemonian stairs (3:84-3:85). Tacitus says he was completing his 57th year (3:86); Suetonius agrees, but Suetonius's own birth date makes him 54, as the Epitome of Dio says (54 years and 89 days). Josephus says he "had his head cut off in the midst of Rome" (War 4.652).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:36; Histories of Tacitus 3:54-3:56; Histories of Tacitus 3:67-3:68; Histories of Tacitus 3:84-3:86

sections.b: In December 69 Domitian is in Rome. Tacitus says he could have escaped but the guards put on him were feared as plotters (3:59), was taken into the Capitol by his uncle Sabinus (3:69), hid with the temple-keeper and got away in a linen robe among worshippers (3:74), and was hailed as Caesar and taken to his father's house (3:86). Suetonius says he escaped dressed as a follower of Isis. Tacitus adds that as emperor he dedicated a temple to Jupiter the Guardian with himself in the god's lap (3:74).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:59; Histories of Tacitus 3:69; Histories of Tacitus 3:74; Histories of Tacitus 3:86

claude.title: Domitian and "Lord and God"
claude.body: Claude's reading of an idea that is not new. Suetonius says a circular letter in the name of Domitian's procurators began, "Our Master and our God bids that this be done" (Domitian 13). Revelation 4:11 praises, "You are worthy, our Lord and God." A common argument for the late date of Revelation, under Domitian, is that the verse answers the emperor's title. Floyd O. Parker (Biblica 82, 2001) argues that the title is Jewish and in the Septuagint and so cannot date the book, and Wikipedia's article on Domitian says Brian Jones thinks the phrases came from flatterers. The note at 3:74 gives the detail.

sections.b: Vespasian is in the East for all of Book 3 and in Egypt by 3:48. He orders the war to wait at Aquileia and rely on Egypt's grain (3:8), is pleased by the news of Cremona and goes to Alexandria (3:48), and receives Antonius's letter (3:53). Tacitus recalls that he had commanded the 2nd legion in Britain under Claudius (3:44); Suetonius says he fought thirty battles there. Josephus says he sent his son Titus to Jerusalem (War 4.658).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:8; Histories of Tacitus 3:44; Histories of Tacitus 3:48; Histories of Tacitus 3:53

sections.b: Mucianus leads the forces of the East but arrives after the fighting. He sends letters urging a victory that would cost "neither blood nor tears" (3:8), writes to Antonius and others in middle-of-the-road terms (3:52), sends the 6th legion against the Dacians (3:46), and holds the victors back with ambiguous letters (3:78). Antonius feuds with him by letter (3:53). Suetonius says he promised Vespasian the Syrian army (Vespasian 6.4); Josephus calls him "president of the province" (War 4.621).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:8; Histories of Tacitus 3:46; Histories of Tacitus 3:52-3:53; Histories of Tacitus 3:78; Acts 11:26

sections.b: Tacitus shows an army that makes and breaks its generals: soldiers choose Antonius (3:3), nearly kill Flavianus and Saturninus (3:10-3:11), swear to a new emperor in one meeting (3:13), demand plunder (3:19, 3:26, 3:32-3:33) and a bonus called the clavarium (3:50), and vote for the centurions they want (3:49). The legions form the tortoise to storm a camp (3:27). The Bible shows the same ranks: a centurion with soldiers under him (Matthew 8:9), the Italian Cohort (Acts 10:1), and tribunes and centurions (Acts 21:31-32).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:3; Histories of Tacitus 3:10-3:13; Histories of Tacitus 3:27; Histories of Tacitus 3:49-3:50; Matthew 8:9; Acts 10:1; Acts 21:31-32; Luke 3:14

sections.b: Praetorian soldiers appear on both sides. Antonius calls them in at the night battle and then calls them "civilians" (3:23-3:24); Vitellius puts the Praetorian prefect Publilius Sabinus in chains and names Alfenus Varus (3:36); Vitellius sends fourteen Praetorian cohorts to hold the Apennines (3:55), leaves part of his forces at Narnia with the Praetorian prefects (3:58), and that army gives up there (3:63). Paul's "whole praetorium" (Philippians 1:13) is read as this guard or a governor's headquarters.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:23-3:24; Histories of Tacitus 3:36; Histories of Tacitus 3:55; Histories of Tacitus 3:58; Histories of Tacitus 3:63; Philippians 1:13

sections.b: Vitellius, speaking to the troops, is covered by a cloud of ill-omened birds, and a bull breaks from the altar (3:56). The Law of Moses forbids looking for omens (Deuteronomy 18:10). In Acts the priest of Zeus at Lystra brings bulls and wreaths to the gates (Acts 14:13), and Jesus speaks of "great signs from the sky" (Luke 21:11).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:56; Deuteronomy 18:10; Acts 14:13; Luke 21:11

sections.b: Gladiators are part of the war. Caecina's show at Cremona helps stir hatred of the town (3:32), Julianus commands gladiators at Tarracina (3:57, 3:76), and the Roman crowd watches the street fighting "as at a game" (3:83). Paul says he "fought with wild beasts at Ephesus" (1 Corinthians 15:32).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:32; Histories of Tacitus 3:57; Histories of Tacitus 3:76; Histories of Tacitus 3:83; 1 Corinthians 15:32

sections.b: Cornelius Fuscus and Portius Septimius are procurators (3:4, 3:5), Valerius Paullinus, a procurator, wins the neighboring communities for Vespasian (3:42), and Fonteius Agrippa governs Asia for a year as proconsul before going to Moesia (3:46). In the Bible Pilate governs Judea (Luke 3:1), Festus takes over from Felix (Acts 24:27), and proconsuls sit at Ephesus, Cyprus and Achaia (Acts 19:38; Acts 13:7; Acts 18:12).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:4-3:5; Histories of Tacitus 3:42; Histories of Tacitus 3:46; Luke 3:1; Acts 24:27; Acts 19:38; Acts 18:12

sections.b: Vitellius, "with no thought for the future," handed out treaties to allies and Latin rights to foreigners, with tribute and duties dropped for some. The wise, Tacitus says, thought that gift worthless. In Acts a commander says, "It cost me a great deal of money to acquire this citizenship," and Paul answers, "I, though, was born to it" (Acts 22:28).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:55; Acts 22:25-28

sections.h: The Senate and consuls in Book 3
sections.b: Tacitus shows the Senate flattering Vitellius (3:37), a man named consul for one day (3:37), the Senate sending envoys to the armies (3:80), and a Senate that could not be called on the last evening (3:86). Years were dated by consuls, as at 3:34 ("in the consulship of Tiberius Sempronius and Publius Cornelius"); Luke dates by reigns (Luke 3:1).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:34; Histories of Tacitus 3:37; Histories of Tacitus 3:80; Histories of Tacitus 3:86; Luke 3:1

sections.b: Roman Knights offer service and money to Vitellius (3:58), crowd Sabinus's house (3:69), and Valens is born into a Knight family (3:62). The Stoic Musonius Rufus, of Knight rank, lectures the soldiers (3:81).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:58; Histories of Tacitus 3:62; Histories of Tacitus 3:69; Histories of Tacitus 3:81

sections.h: Book 3 as the year before the temple fell
sections.b: Book 3 has no Jews and no Judea. It tells the Roman civil war that kept Vespasian away from the Jewish war. Josephus says that after Vitellius fell Vespasian "sent his son Titus, with a select part of his army, to destroy Jerusalem" (War 4.658). After the war Vespasian laid a tribute on Jews "wheresoever they were," two drachmae a year to be paid "into the Capitol, as they used to pay the same to the temple at Jerusalem" (War 7.218). The Capitol that burned in 3:71 had been rebuilt by then.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:71-3:72; Mark 13:2; Luke 21:20; Luke 21:24

claude.title: A pair of fires
claude.body: Claude's own theory: see the topic on the Capitol. The Capitol burned in December 69 and Titus's army took Jerusalem the next year; the two fires belonged to opposite sides of the civil war.

sections.b: Tacitus has Vespasian hurry to Alexandria to hold Egypt's grain and starve Vitellius's side. Josephus says he was "intent upon gaining the dominion over Alexandria" because of the corn (War 4.605-606). Acts names Apollos "an Alexandrian by birth" (Acts 18:24) and a ship "out of Alexandria bound for Italy" (Acts 27:6).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:48; Acts 18:24; Acts 27:6

sections.h: Egypt's grain in the war of 69
sections.b: Vespasian ordered the war to wait because with Egypt, which controls the grain, Vitellius's army could be starved (3:8). Tacitus returns to the plan when Vespasian reaches Alexandria (3:48). In Acts Paul sails to Italy on ships out of Alexandria (Acts 27:6; Acts 28:11).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:8; Histories of Tacitus 3:48; Acts 27:6; Acts 28:11

sections.b: Mucianus governs Syria and brings the eastern forces (3:8, 3:46). The 3rd legion salutes the rising sun, "as is the custom in Syria" (3:24). Antioch in Syria is where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:8; Histories of Tacitus 3:24; Histories of Tacitus 3:46; Acts 11:26

sections.b: Tacitus names Polemon, whose freedman Anicetus raised Pontus in Vitellius's name after it had become a province (3:47). Suetonius says Nero added Pontus to the provinces "when it was given up by Polemon" (Nero 18). Josephus says Berenice "persuaded Poleme, who was king of Cilicia, to be circumcised, and to marry her," that she left him, and that he gave up the marriage and "the Jewish religion" (Antiquities 20.145-146). A Wikipedia page on Polemon II says he ruled Pontus and Cilicia and married Berenice. Likely: Tacitus's Polemon and Berenice's husband are one man.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:47; Acts 25:13; Acts 25:23

sections.b: Josephus's War 4 tells the same year from the East: Vespasian declared emperor (4.601), Alexandria and the corn (4.605-606), Mucianus (4.621), Sabinus taking the Capitol by night (4.645), the temple burned (4.649), Domitian's escape (4.649), and Vitellius's death (4.651-652). He sends Titus to Jerusalem (4.658). He also tells Cremona in a shorter and different form (War 4.11.2-3, Whiston's numbering): Caecina's army deserts and repents, Antonius storms the city and allows the plunder, and Josephus counts 30,200 dead of Vitellius's army against 4,500 of Antonius's men (his figures, not checked against anything else). Antiquities 20.139-146 gives the marriage of Berenice and Polemon (see Tacitus at 3:47).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:8; Histories of Tacitus 3:47; Histories of Tacitus 3:69-3:74; Histories of Tacitus 3:84

sections.h: The sources Tacitus names in Book 3
sections.b: Tacitus names Vipstanus Messalla as his authority for the father and son (3:25) and for one view of who first pointed the soldiers at Cremona (3:28). Gaius Plinius gives the other view, and Tacitus says he cannot easily decide between them (3:28). Cluvius Rufus and Silius Italicus are the two witnesses of the talk between Sabinus and Vitellius (3:65). He also says "I have heard" that Mucianus was glad of Sabinus's death (3:75). Wikipedia says Cluvius Rufus's own history is lost and was a source for Tacitus.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:25; Histories of Tacitus 3:28; Histories of Tacitus 3:65; Histories of Tacitus 3:75

sections.h: Two temples that burned: the Capitol and Jerusalem
sections.b: The Capitol burned in December 69 (3:71-3:72). Solomon's temple, which stood on Mount Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1), burned in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9; 2 Chronicles 36:19), and the Jerusalem temple of Jesus' day fell in AD 70 (Mark 13:2; Luke 21:6). Tacitus calls the Capitol a "pledge of empire." Vespasian later had the Jews' temple tax paid to the Capitol (Josephus, War 7.218).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:71-3:72; 2 Chronicles 3:1; 2 Kings 25:9; Mark 13:2; Luke 21:6

sections.h: Images, titles and gods in Book 3
sections.b: Antonius had the images of the dead Galba put back up in every town (3:7). Vitellius asked to be called Caesar (3:58). Domitian later built a temple to Jupiter the Guardian with himself in the god's lap (3:74), and Suetonius says his officials wrote "Our Master and our God" (Domitian 13). Compare Mark 12:17 and Acts 25:11.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:7; Histories of Tacitus 3:58; Histories of Tacitus 3:74; Mark 12:17; Acts 25:11

sections.h: A bad emperor and the Bible's teaching on rulers
sections.b: The Senate flatters Vitellius (3:37) and he offers his dagger as the sign of life and death (3:68). Paul says, "There is no authority that does not come from God" (Romans 13:1); Peter, "Submit to the king as the one ranked highest" (1 Peter 2:13); and Timothy is to pray "for kings and for all who hold high office" (1 Timothy 2:2). Peter and the apostles also say, "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29). Churches weigh these passages differently, from submission to limits on what rulers may command.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:37; Histories of Tacitus 3:68; Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13; 1 Timothy 2:2; Acts 5:29

sections.b: Vespasian meant to starve his enemy by cutting off the grain. The Bible mentions the great famine "in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28) and lists famines among the signs (Luke 21:11; Matthew 24:7).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:8; Histories of Tacitus 3:48; Acts 11:28; Luke 21:11; Matthew 24:7

sections.b: The soldier who has killed his father without knowing him lifts the body and digs a grave to "do the last duty." A disciple asks Jesus to let him bury his father first (Matthew 8:21-22).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:25; Matthew 8:21; Matthew 8:22

sections.b: The centurion who tells Vitellius the truth about Cremona ends his own life to prove his word. The Bible tells of Saul (1 Samuel 31:4), Ahithophel (2 Samuel 17:23) and Judas (Matthew 27:3-5). Tacitus praises his steadfastness and does not comment on the act itself.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:54; 1 Samuel 31:4; 2 Samuel 17:23; Matthew 27:3; Matthew 27:5

sections.h: The sun salute and the temple of Mefitis (3:24, 3:33)
sections.b: The 3rd legion salutes the rising sun "as is the custom in Syria" (3:24). Moses warned Israel not to be pulled away to bow down to the sun, moon and stars (Deuteronomy 4:19), and Ezekiel saw men at the temple door bowing to the sun (Ezekiel 8:16). At Cremona only the temple of Mefitis stood, "protected by where it stood or by the power of the god" (3:33).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:24; Histories of Tacitus 3:33; Deuteronomy 4:19; Ezekiel 8:16

sections.b: Valens had acted in farces at Nero's Juvenalia (3:62). Vitellius's fall ends the line of emperors Tacitus lists at 3:68: Caesar, Gaius, Nero, Piso, Galba. The site's Revelation page counts these reigns for the seven kings of Revelation 17:10.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:62; Histories of Tacitus 3:68; Revelation 17:10

sections.b: Antonius had Galba's statues put back up (3:7). Tacitus says those who betrayed Vitellius to Vespasian cannot count it a credit, since they had deserted Galba (3:86). Galba's legion, the 7th, is in the Flavianist army (3:7, 3:22).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:7; Histories of Tacitus 3:22; Histories of Tacitus 3:86

sections.h: Soldiers in the Bible and a civil war
sections.b: Book 3 tells of soldiers who plunder, mutiny and kill their own kin. The Gospels tell soldiers, "Don't squeeze money out of anyone by force or by false charges. Make do with your pay" (Luke 3:14). Jesus tells Peter, "Everyone who takes the sword will be destroyed by the sword" (Matthew 26:52), and Pilate hears "My kingdom does not come from this world" (John 18:36). The chapter's card shows how churches answer whether Christians may serve.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:19; Histories of Tacitus 3:25; Histories of Tacitus 3:84; Luke 3:14; Matthew 26:52; John 18:36

sections.h: Client kings and a queen who left her husband
sections.b: Sido and Italicus, kings of the Suevi, are brought over (3:5), and Cartismandua, queen of the Brigantes, leaves her husband for his armor-bearer (3:45). The Bible shows the same Roman arrangement: King Agrippa and Bernice come to Festus (Acts 25:13), and Herod married Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip (Mark 6:17-18).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 3:5; Histories of Tacitus 3:45; Acts 25:13; Mark 6:17
